concept: Nonlinear lead-lag inference: conditional information transfer, finite-sample uncertainty, lag-selection multiplicity and directed graph preservation
summary: Source-anchored research for Nonlinear lead-lag inference: conditional information transfer, finite-sample uncertainty, lag-selection multiplicity and directed graph preservation. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: A surrogate null must match the dependence structure required by the hypothesis. Shorten and colleagues show excessive false positives from naive source time shifts in a common-driver spike-process example; Diks and Fang separately warn that destroying unconditional dependence need not reproduce a conditional-independence null. Their findings concern the tested schemes and processes. (medium confidence)

For time-series significance tests, resampled series must capture the dependence structure compatible with the null hypothesis. The resampling assessment distinguishes constructing an empirical null distribution from merely obtaining a spread of statistic values. (low confidence)

Conditional transfer entropy measures the information supplied by a source history about the target present after conditioning on the target history and specified additional process histories. Fully conditioned TE includes all other measured process histories in that conditioning set. (high confidence)

Interpret TE as a measured directed statistical dependency. A predictive dependency alone does not establish a physical causal mechanism: the estimator study explicitly avoids equating Wiener-style dependency with causal effect, and the high-order TE study distinguishes measured behavior from mechanism. (high confidence)

Bennett, Cucuringu and Reinert describe significance thresholding when constructing a lead-lag network: an edge is retained only when the associated lead-lag metric is sufficiently large. A direction-preserving encoding therefore addresses a different stage from deciding which inferred edges to retain. (low confidence)

James, Barnett and Crutchfield argue that transfer entropy and causation entropy can overestimate information flow or underestimate influence. This is an attributed conceptual limitation, so a predictive dependency should not be presented unconditionally as a physical information-flow magnitude. (low confidence)

Symmetrizing a directed adjacency matrix loses edge orientation. For a lead-lag graph, retaining that symmetrized matrix alone therefore cannot preserve which variable leads which; this application is a methodological inference from the graph representations. (high confidence)

The QuaterGCN authors target unequal antiparallel edge pairs without collapsing them into one edge. The later Haar-Laplacian paper independently identifies a failure of sign-magnetic encoding for reciprocal edges. Thus, support for signed directed inputs alone is insufficient evidence of full graph preservation. (high confidence)

Bennett, Cucuringu and Reinert report low overall persistence and year-to-year instability in their empirical US-equity lead-lag structure. This is a scope warning for carrying an inferred graph across time; it does not measure five-minute SOL graph stability. (low confidence)

For KSG, ordinary resampling with replacement can create duplicate points that appear to be fine-scale information-bearing structure. Holmes and Nemenman show severe upward bias in such bootstrap estimates; Piras and colleagues reproduce this failure. (medium confidence)

Holmes and Nemenman estimate KSG variance using non-overlapping subsamples and a large-sample inverse-sample-size variance model. They warn that overlapping partitions do not supply independent variance samples and that the scaling can fail for small subsamples. Their derivation invokes independent identically distributed contributions; it does not establish validity for autocorrelated lead-lag samples. (low confidence)

McAllester and Stratos prove that a distribution-free, high-confidence lower bound on mutual information from N samples cannot exceed O(ln N). The statement limits such lower confidence bounds; it is not a universal ceiling on every point estimate under additional distributional assumptions. (low confidence)

Bootstrap failure is estimator-specific: Piras and colleagues refit a Gaussian mixture model to each bootstrap realization and return the mean and standard deviation of the resulting MI distribution. In their bivariate-Gaussian comparison, GMM-MI agrees with the ground truth while bootstrapped KSG is biased; this experiment does not establish universal calibration. (medium confidence)
Finite-sample uncertainty in mutual-information estimates includes systematic bias as well as sampling variability; error bars alone do not establish that an estimate is unbiased. (medium confidence)

Holmes and Nemenman recommend checking sample-size drift relative to error bars, checking inverse-sample-size variance scaling, and requiring stability across a range of neighbor counts. They caution against declaring an estimator unbiased from stability over only a small sample-size range. (low confidence)

In the Novelli et al. hierarchy, maximum-statistic control concerns candidate selection for an individual target, while an additional omnibus/FDR layer combines targets. The authors explicitly distinguish this hierarchy from correction across all links: a stronger link can be pruned if its target fails the omnibus test while a weaker link into another target survives. Consequently these error-control families should not be described as interchangeable. (low confidence)

Kořenek, Sanda and Hlinka propose optimally conditioned TE to distinguish a genuinely synergistic causal set from separate individual causes: for exclusive disjunction, their abstract assigns the role to the multivariate set rather than the individual inputs. This is an attributed proposal, not a universal interpretation of standard conditional TE. (low confidence)

Baboukani and colleagues propose reducing dimensionality through non-uniform embedding before estimating directed dependencies. This is a proposed estimator design, rather than evidence that arbitrary history embeddings identify the same quantity. (low confidence)

Transfer entropy has a model-free information-theoretic formulation that can assess linear and nonlinear interactions; nonlinear sensitivity depends on using an estimator appropriate to the dependence rather than imposing a linear-Gaussian model. JIDT documents KSG, kernel and linear-Gaussian estimator families. (high confidence)

Additional conditioning does not necessarily reduce TE: redundant information can be removed, whereas synergistic information can become accessible. Conditional TE therefore includes source-unique information and source-conditioner synergy, rather than isolating only a pure two-variable contribution. (high confidence)

Stramaglia and colleagues propose searching conditioning subsets that minimize and maximize TE, rather than relying only on pairwise or fully conditioned TE, to expose redundant and synergistic effects. Their decomposition is a specific analysis proposal and should be identified as such. (low confidence)

The Deep Fusion seed paper explicitly symmetrizes its directed adjacency matrix to use node embeddings. This is a material loss for directional lead–lag interpretation: Bennett, Cucuringu and Reinert explain that naive symmetrization-based clustering uses edge density rather than edge direction. (medium confidence)

MSGNN supplies a directly relevant application: its authors introduce datasets built from financial time-series lead-lag relationships alongside a spectral architecture for signed directed graphs. This establishes application relevance, rather than proving that any inferred edge is causal. (low confidence)

The Haar-Laplacian construction combines symmetric and skew-symmetric adjacency parts into a Hermitian encoding; adding those parts reconstructs the original adjacency. Its stated graph setup excludes self-loops. For a preservation audit, this supplies a concrete reversible construction within those assumptions, rather than a claim about every graph format or normalization. (low confidence)

Novelli and colleagues evaluate inferred directed networks using synthetic linear and nonlinear dynamics. They report that varying the significance threshold changes the precision-recall tradeoff, with more favorable tradeoffs for longer time series. This concerns inference reliability, separately from whether a graph representation retains direction. (low confidence)

Finite-sample information estimates can exaggerate weak dependence. Kirkley identifies positive plug-in transfer-entropy bias with sparse bin counts; Chrisman illustrates positive empirical mutual-information bias at weak or absent dependence. These are estimator-specific findings, rather than a universal sign rule for every estimator. (medium confidence)

Papana and colleagues find a specificity-sensitivity tradeoff across their resampling settings: more random resampling makes the partial-transfer-entropy test more conservative, and none of their first six methods is optimal across the tested systems. They also report residual spurious couplings in some nonlinear settings. (low confidence)

GMM-MI provides a concrete implementation of model-based mutual-information uncertainty using Gaussian mixtures and bootstrap. Its authors benchmark finite-sample estimates against known distributions. This supplies an implementation candidate, rather than demonstrated confidence-interval coverage for autocorrelated trading data. (medium confidence)

Searching candidate lags and then testing the selected lag as though it were fixed creates a multiplicity problem. Include lag selection in the inferential procedure rather than reporting an unadjusted selected-lag test. (high confidence)

Conditioning does not necessarily reduce measured dependence: conditional information can increase or decrease. Therefore a fully conditioned value and a pairwise value answer different predictive questions. (low confidence)

Bivariate TE can reflect indirect influences or shared drivers. Conditioning on relevant observed processes can separate those effects from the source-target dependency; the interpretation is relative to the variables and histories actually included. (high confidence)

Keskin and Aste use Schreiber’s general non-parametric formulation to quantify nonlinear transfer entropy, contrasting it with the autoregressive formulation used for linear transfer entropy. (low confidence)
The JIDT repository records adding conditional-transfer-entropy calculators implemented through underlying conditional-mutual-information calculators. (low confidence)

JIDT provides transfer entropy, mutual information and their conditional variants for discrete and continuous data, with Java implementations usable from languages including Python and R. This README establishes toolkit scope; it does not establish any particular installed version or estimator configuration. (low confidence)

MagNet encodes direction in complex phase, but setting its charge parameter q to zero reduces it to adjacency symmetrization; using a magnetic operator alone therefore does not ensure that direction is retained. (low confidence)

The SigMaNet authors introduce a parameter-free Sign-Magnetic Laplacian for directed graphs whose weights can have either sign and unrestricted magnitude. This is an attributed design claim, not a guarantee for every directed topology. (low confidence)

The QuaterGCN authors identify unequal-weight antiparallel edge pairs as a preservation requirement: their Quaternionic Laplacian represents those pairs without reducing them to one directed or undirected edge. Their claim scopes the broader idea that encoding edge direction necessarily preserves the whole weighted graph. (low confidence)

Fitch constructs an undirected symmetrization with the same pairwise effective resistances as its directed input. This is a specific metric-preservation guarantee; it does not state that the undirected output retains each edge orientation. (low confidence)

NetworkX issue 8560 proposes magnetic_laplacian_matrix and magnetic_laplacian_spectrum for directed spectral analysis. The issue is implementation-discussion evidence; it does not establish that either function shipped in a release. (low confidence)

MagNet encodes directional information in complex phase, while entry magnitudes encode undirected geometry. Encoding direction is a representation property and should be checked separately from preserving all reciprocal edge weights. (medium confidence)

The SigMaNet authors describe a parameter-free sign-magnetic Laplacian for directed and undirected graphs with unrestricted weight sign and magnitude, and report that its direction encoding avoids a weight-magnitude problem of other Laplacians. This does not establish preservation of every reciprocal weight pair. (low confidence)

The cited NetworkX documentation snapshot states that converting a directed graph to an undirected graph can collapse differing reciprocal edge data to one arbitrarily chosen value. This supports the conclusion that the conversion alone does not preserve both directional weights; it does not establish behavior for every historical package release. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

For KSG, Holmes and Nemenman propose checking whether the estimate drifts with sample size relative to its sampling standard deviation. Drift substantially exceeding that deviation indicates bias; this diagnostic does not by itself justify extrapolating and subtracting an unknown bias curve. (low confidence)

For finite-cardinality streams, Kirkley proposes a finite-data transfer-entropy measure asymptotically equivalent to the standard plug-in estimator and describes a nonparametric significance assessment without simulation. The cited abstract scopes this to small samples or high cardinality; it does not validate continuous financial time series. (low confidence)

A maximum-statistic test mirrors candidate selection: calculate the maximum across candidate surrogate statistics in each surrogate realization, then compare the observed selected maximum against that distribution. The IDTxl paper describes this procedure and its pinned implementation constructs a surrogate table and tests against its maxima. (high confidence)

The multi-lag truncated time-shift procedure tests a specified set of candidate lags and applies Bonferroni correction: each lag uses the overall significance level divided by the number of tested lags. The authors state that this preserves the validity of the procedure. (medium confidence)

A broader lag range has a cost in the multi-lag truncated time-shift procedure: Bonferroni correction increases the minimum truncation radius, and longer time series may be needed. Restricting the search range with prior knowledge therefore has practical value within this procedure. (low confidence)

For the truncated time-shift test, a lag may be chosen from a mechanistic hypothesis or independent pilot data. Selecting the preshift from the same observations and applying the ordinary fixed-lag test is specifically discouraged by the authors. (low confidence)

Choose the permutation budget to resolve the multiplicity-adjusted significance threshold. The filtering-and-downsampling study explicitly links the minimum attainable p-value to the number of permutations and statistical comparisons; the pinned IDTxl implementation floors a zero empirical tail fraction at the reciprocal of the surrogate count and uses a strict p-value threshold. (high confidence)
